2.text: adjacent countries. Thus, among the Koryak, Reindeer and Maritime, the

3.text: wife is obtained by service in her family. Among the ancient Kamchadal,

4.text: according to Steller, when somebody wanted to marry, he could get a wife

5.text: merely by serving a term in her family. The details of the service are

6.text: quite similar to those existing among the Chukchee. The young man must

7.text: perform the hardest tasks of the household; and often, if he gives no satis-

8.text: faction, he must go away without a word, and all his work is lost, to no

10.text: Among the Aleut the young man was obliged to live with his wife’s

11.text: parents and to serve them.² The custom of service exists also among the Ainu.³
11.note: Both footnote markers confirmed superscript (², ³) at 2x; machine text had '?' and ASCII '3'.

12.text: Young single men among the Maritime Chukchee, as well as among the

13.text: reindeer-breeding branch of the tribe, enter as adopted sons-in-law into more

14.text: prosperous families with many daughters. Finally, group-marriages and levirate

15.text: are as fully developed as among the Reindeer Chukchee. Mixed marriages

16.text: with persons belonging to another people are as common among the Maritime

17.text: Chukchee as among the Reindeer branch. I have referred to the frequent

18.text: mixed marriages between the Maritime and the Reindeer Chukchee.⁴ Marriages
18.note: Footnote marker confirmed superscript ⁴ at 2x.

19.text: between the Maritime Chukchee and the Asiatic Eskimo are almost as common.

25.text: repeated by the Chukchee all over their territory. Wives from the American

26.text: shores are met less frequently among the Maritime Chukchee, and vice versa.

27.text: In regard to the “prostitution of hospitality,” it should be said, that,

28.text: under the influence of American whalers, paid prostitution has developed

29.text: among all the Maritime peoples on both coasts of Bering Sea. During the

30.text: entire voyage, each ship has on board several young women from the Asiatic

31.text: or the American shore. I have witnessed how, on the arrival of an American

32.text: ship at the village Uñiˊsak, women in skin boats approached it from all sides,
32.resolved: Uñiˊsak: ñ = n+U+0303; ˊ = U+02CA (stress) after i.

33.text: offering themselves quite openly. In order to be better understood, they

34.text: would press their hands to their cheeks and close the eyes, symbolizing sleep.

35.text: The marriage-rite consists of a sacrifice to the hearth and a general

36.text: anointment. Instead of blood, red ochre is used for anointing. Whenever I

37.text: asked what marks the married couple painted on their faces, the answer,

38.text: curiously enough, was invariably “Tŭmñ-aˊlvalag̣” (“It makes no difference”).
